title: Pigments: a timeline in colour
summary: Every colour has a birthday. Learn the dates that matter — and why they can disprove a date but never prove an author.

shots.title:
Every colour
has a birthday.
shots.subtitle: A painting can't be older than its **youngest** paint.
shots.narration: Many pigments were invented on a known date. A painting cannot be older than the newest material in it — and that simple rule has unmasked famous forgeries.

shots.text: **Lead white**: the painter's white until the 19th century.
shots.narration: For centuries, painters' white was lead white, basic lead carbonate. It remained the main white pigment until the nineteenth century.

shots.text: **Ultramarine**, ground from lapis lazuli mined in Afghanistan.
shots.narration: The richest blue, natural ultramarine, was ground from lapis lazuli mined in Badakhshan in Afghanistan, and was the most expensive blue. An artificial version arrived in the nineteenth century.

Then came the chemists. Prussian blue in 1704; cobalt blue and zinc white in the early 1800s; chrome yellow and emerald green soon after; cadmiums around 1840; titanium white from 1918; phthalocyanines in the 1930s.

shots.text: **Prussian blue** in a sky dated 1650? A problem.
shots.narration: Prussian blue, discovered in 1704, is the oldest modern synthetic pigment. Find it in the original paint of a sky dated 1650, and the date is impossible.

shots.text: **Titanium white**: produced from 1918, sold to artists from 1920.
shots.narration: Titanium white is the key twentieth-century marker. It was first produced in Norway in 1918; artists could buy it as paint from 1920 in America and by 1924 in Europe.

shots.text: Introduction dates are **disputed in detail**. Use the earliest plausible date.
shots.narration: Be careful with dates. Sources disagree in detail: one standard reference puts the first artists' titanium white in Europe in 1919, with experimental use before 1916. Always use the earliest plausible date.
And availability isn't popularity. In a survey of 184 paintings from 1920 to the 1990s, titanium white turned up in only sixteen, and was extremely rare before the 1940s.

shots.text: **Terminus post quem**: the date after which the painting must have been made.
shots.narration: Historians call this lower bound the terminus post quem. It can prove a date impossible. On its own, it can never prove a painting genuine.

props.question: A survey analysed **184** paintings made between 1920 and the 1990s. In how many did it find titanium white?
props.reveal: Only sixteen. Titanium white was on the market from 1920 but stayed extremely rare in paintings until the 1940s — so its absence from an early-20th-century work proves nothing, and its presence is a strong date marker.

questions.prompt: The original paint of a sky dated 1650 contains Prussian blue. What follows?
options: The painter must have been Prussian
questions.explain: Prussian blue dates from 1704. Only a later retouching could explain it — which is why examiners check where the sample came from.

questions.prompt: What does a terminus post quem give you?
options: The latest date a painting could be made
The earliest date a painting could have been made
questions.explain: It is a lower bound from the newest material present.

questions.prompt: No anachronistic pigment is found. The painting is…
options: consistent with its date — not proven genuine
questions.explain: Pigment dating gives relative information only; a careful forger can use period materials.

questions.prompt: In which year was titanium white first produced (in Norway)?
questions.explain: US production followed a year later; artists' paint from 1920 in the USA.
